title: Anti-inflammatory Effects of Matricaria chamomilla Extracts on BALB/c Mice Macrophages and Lymphocytes.
summary: Measured apigenin and total phenols in aqueous and alcoholic chamomile extracts and tested them on mouse macrophages and lymphocytes. The authors reported reduced nitric oxide production with both extracts, a Th1 shift with the aqueous extract, and a stronger anti-inflammatory effect for the alcoholic extract.
comparison: Related water-based preparation, but not an exact match: the Sharr study records an infusion of aerial parts; the abstract describes a prepared aqueous extract and does not state the plant part or extraction method.
limitation: Cells isolated from mice, tested in the laboratory; not a human study. The abstract does not report outcomes for the infections recorded in the Sharr study.

title: Hypericum perforatum and Its Potential Antiplatelet Effect.
preparation: Hypericum perforatum extracts (solvent and plant part not stated in the abstract)
summary: Used flow cytometry to look at platelet activation markers in the presence of St John's wort extracts. The authors reported a possible inhibitory effect on platelet activation linked to intracellular calcium mobilization and activated GPIIbIIIa receptor expression.
comparison: Preparation match unconfirmed: the Sharr study records an infusion of aerial parts, but the abstract does not say how the extracts were made. The topic relates to the anticoagulant use recorded in the Sharr study.
limitation: In-vitro platelet study only; the authors themselves note the limits of an in-vitro study and call for further work. Not evidence of an effect on bleeding or clotting in people.

title: Urtica dioica Leaf Infusion Enhances the Sensitivity of Triple-Negative Breast Cancer Cells to Cisplatin Treatment.
summary: Tested nettle tea combined with cisplatin on MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells. The authors reported that the combination reduced cell proliferation more than either treatment alone, with markers of apoptosis.
comparison: Same preparation type (infusion) as the Sharr record, but the paper used leaves while the Sharr study records aerial parts; equivalence of plant material and infusion method is unconfirmed.
limitation: Single cancer cell line in the laboratory, tested together with a chemotherapy drug. It does not show that nettle tea treats cancer in people and does not test it as a standalone remedy.

title: Investigation on anti-Corona viral potential of Yarrow tea.
preparation: Yarrow tea (herbal tea of flowers and leaves, as described in the abstract)
summary: Combined network pharmacology, metabolite analysis, docking and molecular simulation to study yarrow tea constituents in relation to Covid-19 genes, and examined yarrow-treated virus by electron microscopy. The authors propose luteolin acting on PTGS2 (cyclooxygenase II) as a possible anti-inflammatory mechanism and report disintegration of the virus membrane.
comparison: Tea is the same preparation type as the infusion recorded in the Sharr study; whether the tested tea matches the Sharr plant material and method is unconfirmed. Relates loosely to the influenza use recorded, not to Covid-19 specifically.
limitation: Mostly computational (in-silico) predictions plus a microscopy assay; no animal or human testing. Mechanisms proposed are hypotheses, not demonstrated treatment effects.

title: Thymus serpyllum Exhibits Anti-Diabetic Potential in Streptozotocin-Induced Diabetes Mellitus Type 2 Mice: A Combined Biochemical and In Vivo Study.
summary: Gave an aqueous wild thyme extract to mice with diet- and streptozotocin-induced type 2 diabetes for four weeks. The authors reported better control of blood glucose, improved glucose and insulin tolerance, and upregulation of AMPK, IRS1 and GLUT2 gene expression.
comparison: Related water-based preparation, but the abstract does not say whether it is an infusion or which plant part was used; the Sharr study records an infusion of aerial parts. The diabetes outcome is not one of the uses recorded for this plant in the Sharr study (it lists an anticholesterolemic use).
limitation: Animal study in a chemically induced diabetes model; not evidence of benefit in people. Group sizes are not given in the abstract.

title: Effects of Salvia officinalis L. (common sage) leaves tea on insulin resistance, lipid profile, and oxidative stress in rats with polycystic ovary: An experimental study.
preparation: Sage leaf tea given to rats in place of drinking water
summary: Gave sage tea instead of water to rats with testosterone-induced polycystic ovary syndrome. The authors reported higher serum total antioxidant capacity and lower glucose, total cholesterol, LDL-C and atherogenic index, with no change in insulin, triglycerides, VLDL-C or MDA.
comparison: Close preparation match: a leaf tea, similar to the sage infusion in the Sharr study, though the Sharr record adds honey and lists aerial parts. Relates to the anti-diabetic use recorded; the PCOS model itself is not part of the Sharr record.
limitation: Small animal study (6 rats per group) in an induced PCOS model; not a human study. The abstract reports a decrease in HDL-C alongside the other changes.

title: Hepatoprotective and antioxidant activity of linden (Tilia platyphyllos L.) infusion against ethanol-induced oxidative stress in rats.
preparation: Infusion of linden flowers given as a beverage
summary: Tested a linden flower infusion in rats exposed to ethanol and measured liver damage markers and antioxidant defense components. Some serum markers decreased in the ethanol plus linden group, but the authors concluded the infusion did not restore lipid peroxidation or the antioxidant system and may not be as important as diet-derived antioxidants.
comparison: Close match: a flower infusion, the same plant part and preparation type recorded in the Sharr study; equivalence of material and method is unconfirmed. The liver outcome is not one of the uses recorded for this plant in the Sharr study.
limitation: Animal study with mixed or negative results; the abstract also reports some marker increases in the linden-only group. Not evidence of benefit in people.

title: Mentha pulegium Aqueous Extract Exhibits Antidiabetic and Hepatoprotective Effects in Streptozotocin-Induced Diabetic Rats.
preparation: Aqueous extract of aerial parts given orally
summary: Tested an aqueous extract of pennyroyal aerial parts in normal and streptozotocin-diabetic rats. The authors reported lower blood glucose in diabetic rats, improved glucose tolerance in normal rats, and beneficial changes in liver and pancreas tissue.
comparison: Same plant part (aerial parts) and a water-based preparation, but the abstract does not say whether it is an infusion as recorded in the Sharr study. Blood sugar is not among the uses recorded for this plant in the Sharr study.
limitation: Small animal study (6 rats per group); not a human study. Pennyroyal safety is not assessed in this abstract.
